item.title: Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes
item.description:
Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes

The Weaviate Helm chart has released version 17.1.0, introducing significant updates to cluster bootstrapping in Weaviate v1.25 and removing default resource constraints to improve module performance.

🔍 Overview

Weaviate can be deployed to a Kubernetes cluster using the provided Helm chart, provided that Helm is installed. Version 17.1.0 of the chart addresses specific infrastructure changes required by newer Weaviate releases and resolves performance restrictions in default configurations.

⚙️ Key Details: Cluster Bootstrapping

Weaviate v1.25 introduced a significant change in how the cluster bootstraps, driven by the adoption of a Raft-based consensus model.

  • The podManagementPolicy was changed from OrderedReady to Parallel.
  • This change is required for the Raft cluster to bootstrap properly, as all pods must start simultaneously.
  • Once the Raft cluster is established, rolling updates are possible.
  • This change takes effect when migrating from versions prior to v1.25 or when bootstrapping a new v1.25 cluster.

⚠️ Migration Steps

When upgrading from a version older than v1.25 to v1.25 or above, the following one-time operation is required:

  1. Delete Weaviate’s Statefulset.
  2. Update the Statefulset settings to reflect the new policy.

This process will not remove your data but is necessary to make the update of Statefulset settings possible.

📉 Key Details: Resource Limits

In Weaviate-Helm version 17.1.0, the default resource limits and requests defined in the values.yml file have been removed.

  • Reason: Previous default values restricted the performance of some modules, making them almost unusable unless resources.requests and resources.limits were overridden.
  • Impact: Modules deployed with default values prior to version 17.1.0 will have their resource values removed upon upgrading to 17.1.0 or above, resulting in no constraints on memory or CPU usage.
  • Recommendation: To prevent modules from consuming all system resources, users are strongly recommended to override modules.$MODULE.resources.requests and modules.$MODULE.resources.limits with values that suit their specific system.

🛠 Release Process

To release a new version of the chart, the following steps are taken:

  • Bump the chart version in ./weaviate/Chart.yaml.
  • Create a commit and an annotated tag matching the version number (prefixed with v, e.g., v1.4.3).
  • Push the commit and tag to the repository.
  • A GitHub Action creates a drafted release with the packaged chart attached.
  • The draft is edited to include release notes and published.

#Weaviate #Kubernetes #Helm #VectorDB #DevOps

item.title: Weaviate Releases Idiomatic Go Client Library
item.description:
Weaviate Releases Idiomatic Go Client Library

Weaviate has published an idiomatic Go client library for interacting with its vector database platform.

🔍 Overview

  • The Go client provides a native interface for Weaviate’s core features and APIs
  • Example code is available demonstrating key functionality
  • Full documentation covers usage patterns and integration details

📚 Resources

  • Examples: Located in the example directory showing core features and API usage
  • Documentation: Available at docs.weaviate.io covering Weaviate concepts and Go client specifics

item.title: Weaviate Moves Documentation to a New Dedicated Repository
item.description:
Weaviate Moves Documentation to a New Dedicated Repository

The documentation for the Weaviate project has been moved to a new repository at weaviate/docs and is now live at https://docs.weaviate.io. The updated documentation platform uses Docusaurus 2, a static website generator running under Node.js, and uses the yarn project management tool to manage dependencies.

⚙️ Key details

The documentation build system leverages several tools and configuration specifications:

  • Docusaurus 2: A static website generator running under Node.js that builds the site and generates static content into the build directory.
  • Node.js: Installed via the nvm package manager. While nvm installs the most recent version of Node.js by default, contributors should install the version specified in .github/workflows/pull_requests.yaml (which is version 20 at the time of writing).
  • Yarn & npm: The npm package manager, which is included with Node.js, is used to install yarn. In turn, yarn is used to install Docusaurus and manage project dependencies.
  • Code Formats: Code examples in the documentation are presented in one of two formats, with many utilizing a custom FilteredTextBlock JSX component.

🧩 How to Contribute

Contributors can update the documentation by setting up a local development environment and submitting changes through GitHub:

  1. Fork and Clone: Fork the upstream repository at https://github.com/weaviate/weaviate-io and clone it locally.
  2. Set Tracking Branches: Set the remote tracking branch to monitor upstream changes. When creating a new project branch, add upstream/main as a tracking branch.
  3. Install Dependencies: Switch to the project directory and run yarn to update and install dependencies.
  4. Run a Local Server: Start the yarn server to build the site and launch a local preview at http://localhost:3000/. The server can be stopped by closing the terminal or pressing Ctrl+C/Cmd+C.
  5. Verify and Submit: Double-check all links before submitting a merge request. Working links should be removed from the URL_IGNORES list, while broken links should be reported directly in the pull request against the upstream/main branch.

#Weaviate #Docusaurus #OpenSource #Documentation
